CARRIERS OF THE MAGNETIZATION We unsuccessfully attempted to leach a few limestone sam- ples in order to identify magnetic minerals in the residue; only an occasional pyrite grain was observed in addition to the nonferrous minerals. More successful was the technique of imparting an isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) to the carbonate samples. As discussed by Dunlop [1972] and Heller [1978], acquisition of IRM can be quite diagnostic be- cause the coercivities of magnetite, hematite, and goethite generally differ significantly. Figure 11 shows IRM acquisi- tion curves for a representative set of samples from the sedi- mentary units. With the exception of two red limestone sam- ples, all samples reach saturation at or below _<0.3 T (3000 G), a result indicating titanomagnetite or magnetite as the princi- pal carriers of the magnetization. We assume that these mag- netites are detrital or of early bacterial origin and that there- fore most of the observed characteristic directions are primary. CARRIERS OF THE MAGNETIZATION We unsuccessfully attempted to leach a few limestone sam- ples in order to identify magnetic minerals in the residue; only an occasional pyrite grain was observed in addition to the nonferrous minerals. More successful was the technique of imparting an isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) to the carbonate samples. As discussed by Dunlop [1972] and Heller [1978], acquisition of IRM can be quite diagnostic be- cause the coercivities of magnetite, hematite, and goethite generally differ significantly. Figure 11 shows IRM acquisi- tion curves for a representative set of samples from the sedi- mentary units. Monger and Ross showed that the late Paleozoic clastic and volcanic rocks of the eastern and western belts are rather similar but differ sig- nificantly from those of the central belt, and mentioned that blueschist-facies metamorphic rocks occur locally between the central and eastern belts. Two alternative plate-tectonic models to account for the juxtaposition of these three belts were also offered by Monger and Ross [1971]. In the first model, the eastern and western belts formed above subduction zones of opposite polarity while the central belt formed near the intervening spreading center; the three belts then collapsed together with the cessa- tion of spreading and accelerated subduction of the oceanic crust. As discussed by Dunlop [1972] and Heller [1978], acquisition of IRM can be quite diagnostic be- cause the coercivities of magnetite, hematite, and goethite generally differ significantly. CARRIERS OF THE MAGNETIZATION We unsuccessfully attempted to leach a few limestone sam- ples in order to identify magnetic minerals in the residue; only an occasional pyrite grain was observed in addition to the nonferrous minerals. More successful was the technique of imparting an isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) to the carbonate samples. As discussed by Dunlop [1972] and Heller [1978], acquisition of IRM can be quite diagnostic be- cause the coercivities of magnetite, hematite, and goethite generally differ significantly. Figure 11 shows IRM acquisi- tion curves for a representative set of samples from the sedi- mentary units. With the exception of two red limestone sam- ples, all samples reach saturation at or below _<0.3 T (3000 G), a result indicating titanomagnetite or magnetite as the princi- pal carriers of the magnetization. Monger and Ross showed that the late Paleozoic clastic and volcanic rocks of the eastern and western belts are rather similar but differ sig- nificantly from those of the central belt, and mentioned that blueschist-facies metamorphic rocks occur locally between the central and eastern belts. Fifteen sites within the Caribbean Mountains have easterly declina- tions with shallow, mixed positive and negative inclinations. rocks of Mesozoic age from the Caribbean area have frequently demon- strated anomalous equatorial or subequatorial paleomagnetic pole positions [MacDonald and Opdyke, 1972]. These are anomalous in view of abundant data from rocks of both North and South America which establish the existence of a high- latitude paleomagnetic pole for the Mesozoic (see data in the work of McElhinney [1973]). Watkins and Cambray [1970], Fink and Harrison [1971], Guja and Vincenz [1971], and Vincenz et al. The Hickory mem- ber of the Riley Formation represents a basal transgressive sequence, which overlies the Pre- cambrian crystalline basement with a profound unconformity. Late Middle Cambrian (Albertan) trilobite species of Bolaspidella are found low in this unit, whereas the sampled upper portions of the Hickory are Dresbachian in age. The sam- pled strata consisted of hematitic sandstones which have potential for economic exploitation [Barnes and Schofield, 1964]. The origin and age of the hematite is problematic, since it coats detrital grains and fills interstices between grain boundaries. Biogeneric fragments appear to have been entirely replaced by hematite so at least a portion of the hematite is not detrital. It has been suggested by Barnes and Schofield [1964] that the hematite was formed from iron contained in iron oxy-hydroxides (goethite, limonite, etc.) which was later transformed into hemretire upon burial. The Hickory mem- ber of the Riley Formation represents a basal transgressive sequence, which overlies the Pre- cambrian crystalline basement with a profound unconformity. Late Middle Cambrian (Albertan) trilobite species of Bolaspidella are found low in this unit, whereas the sampled upper portions of the Hickory are Dresbachian in age. The sam- pled strata consisted of hematitic sandstones which have potential for economic exploitation [Barnes and Schofield, 1964]. The origin and age of the hematite is problematic, since it coats detrital grains and fills interstices between grain boundaries. Biogeneric fragments appear to have been entirely replaced by hematite so at least a portion of the hematite is not detrital. It has been suggested by Barnes and Schofield [1964] that the hematite was formed from iron contained in iron oxy-hydroxides (goethite, limonite, etc.) which was later transformed into hemretire upon burial. Replacement of chamosite and glauconite may also have been responsible. Conformably overlying the Hickory in a grada- tional contact is the Cap Mountain Limestone Member of the Riley Formation. We will consider the results from the Llano uplift of Texas in the context of these possi- bilities. The southeasterly declinations of the members older than the Point Peak Shale could be considered as the vector sum of a southerly late Paleozoic/early Mesozoic compon- ent and an easterly Cambrian component [Reeve, 1975]. However, the normal polarity directions (with northwest declinations) observed in the Cap Mountain Member in this study argue against this interpretation. If these magnetizations were the vector sum of a normal polarity Cam- brian component and a southerly late Paleozoic/ early Mesozoic component, the declinations would be drawn toward the southwest not the northwest. A secondary component with northerly declinations remains a possibility, but it would be fortuitous if normal polarity Cambrian com- ponents would be overprinted by normal polarity late Paleozoic/early Mesozoic components, while all reversed Cambrian components are overprinted by reversed secondary components. In addition, the late Paleozoic has an overwhelming dominance of reversed (Kiaman) directions. DIGICO complete result magnetometers [Molyneux, 1971] were used to measure the remanent magnetization of speci- mens and to compute the Fisher [1953] statistics and pole posi- tions. Stepwise demagnetization was carried out using Schonstedt alternating field (af) and thermal demagnetizers (models GSD-1 and TSD-1, respectively). A low-field, 217-Hz excitation frequency transformer bridge, capable of heating and cooling specimens while monitoring susceptibility, was used for Curie temperature estimates. SAMPLING AND TECHNIQUES The areas sampled are shown in Figure 1. A portable field drill was used to collect oriented cores from each of the bodies sampled, and the cores were oriented using both a sun com- pass and a magnetic compass. DIGICO complete result magnetometers [Molyneux, 1971] were used to measure the remanent magnetization of speci- mens and to compute the Fisher [1953] statistics and pole posi- tions. Stepwise demagnetization was carried out using Schonstedt alternating field (af) and thermal demagnetizers (models GSD-1 and TSD-1, respectively). A low-field, 217-Hz excitation frequency transformer bridge, capable of heating and cooling specimens while monitoring susceptibility, was used for Curie temperature estimates. Orthogonal projections [Zijderveld, 1967] have been employed throughout to facilitate the recognition of discrete magnetic components, while vector subtraction [Roy and Park, 1974] has been utilized to estimate the directions of components removed by stepwise cleaning procedures. Some smaller (up to a few millimeters in diameter) basaltic fragments were physically separated, and after examination of the k-T curves and a com- parison with curves for the breccia, they were found to carry a minor fraction of the magnetization of the breccia as a whole. SAMPLING AND TECHNIQUES The areas sampled are shown in Figure 1. A portable field drill was used to collect oriented cores from each of the bodies sampled, and the cores were oriented using both a sun com- pass and a magnetic compass. Approximately six samples (cores) were collected from each site, and the samples were sliced into several specimens with approximate dimensions of 22-mm height x 25-mm diameter. DIGICO complete result magnetometers [Molyneux, 1971] were used to measure the remanent magnetization of speci- mens and to compute the Fisher [1953] statistics and pole posi- tions. Stepwise demagnetization was carried out using Schonstedt alternating field (af) and thermal demagnetizers (models GSD-1 and TSD-1, respectively). A low-field, 217-Hz excitation frequency transformer bridge, capable of heating and cooling specimens while monitoring susceptibility, was used for Curie temperature estimates. Orthogonal projections [Zijderveld, 1967] have been employed throughout to facilitate the recognition of discrete magnetic components, while vector subtraction [Roy and Park, 1974] has been utilized to estimate the directions of components removed by stepwise cleaning procedures. he lower part of the Mackenzie Moun- tains Supergroup) comprising the unnamed H1 unit to the Little Dal Group, and including the basic intrusions which cut all these units, is thought to be largely Helikian in age through tentative correlation of lithologies with the Belt-Purcell Super- group of southern British Columbia and Alberta and north- western United States [Gabrielse, 1967, 1972]. An uncon- formity above the Little Dal Group [Eisbacher, 1978] supposedly marks the beginning of the Hadrynian succession, which in part includes the remaining rock units of the Mac- kenzie Mountains Supergroup-the Redstone River and Cop- percap Formations. The Rapitan Group, separated from the Coppercap Formation by a profound unconformity [Ga- brielse, 1967], is thought to be equivalent to the Windermere Supergroup of southwestern British Columbia. Sedimentation of the Belt-Purcell and Windermere rocks probably took place within the broad limits of about 1600 to 850 Ma and 850 to 570 Ma respectively [Gabrielse, 1972; Hofmann and Aitken, 1979]. Additional lithological correlations have also been made with rocks north of Great Bear Lake: those of the Brock Inlier, the Coppermine area, and Victoria and Banks Islands [see Young, 1977]; but these stratigraphic successions like those o

own range of Chuaria, now known to range back into strata as old as 1600 Ma in China (J. D. Aitken, personal communication, 1979). The only pertinent radiometric dates available are Rb- Sr isochron dates of 766 _+ 24 Ma and 769 _+ 27 Ma (3 -- 1.42 X 10 -l yr -l) from two gabbroic sills in the Tsezotene Forma- tion which are probably related to intrusions that cut the 'ba- sinal sequence' and at least as high as the overlying 'grain- stone subunit' (R. L. Armstrong et al., manuscript in preparation 1980; J. D. Aitken, personal communication, 1979). Young et al. [1979] assign the Little Dal Group to a su- pra-regional sequence deposited between  1.2 and 0.8 Ga ago. All the major units of the Helikian succession save H 1 were sampled, as well as possible correlatives in the Brock Inlier (Figure 2); but only results from the Little Dal Group are pre- sented here. Major folding occurred in the Helikian succes- sion of the Mackenzie Mountains in Paleocene or pre-late Cretaceous times. Displacements of the Little Dal Group at the Mackenzie Mountain Front relative to the Canadian Shield are estimated to have been less than 10 km in total [Ait- ken et al., 1980]. he lower part of the Mackenzie Moun- tains Supergroup) comprising the unnamed H1 unit to the Little Dal Group, and including the basic intrusions which cut all these units, is thought to be largely Helikian in age through tentative correlation of lithologies with the Belt-Purcell Super- group of southern British Columbia and Alberta and north- western United States [Gabrielse, 1967, 1972]. An uncon- formity above the Little Dal Group [Eisbacher, 1978] supposedly marks the beginning of the Hadrynian succession, which in part includes the remaining rock units of the Mac- kenzie Mountains Supergroup-the Redstone River and Cop- percap Formations. The Rapitan Group, separated from the Coppercap Formation by a profound unconformity [Ga- brielse, 1967], is thought to be equivalent to the Windermere Supergroup of southwestern British Columbia. Sedimentation of the Belt-Purcell and Windermere rocks probably took place within the broad limits of about 1600 to 850 Ma and 850 to 570 Ma respectively [Gabrielse, 1972; Hofmann and Aitken, 1979]. Additional lithological correlations have also been made with rocks north of Great Bear Lake: those of the Brock Inlier, the Coppermine area, and Victoria and Banks Islands [see Young, 1977]; but these stratigraphic successions like those o

own range of Chuaria, now known to range back into strata as old as 1600 Ma in China (J. D. Aitken, personal communication, 1979). The only pertinent radiometric dates available are Rb- Sr isochron dates of 766 _+ 24 Ma and 769 _+ 27 Ma (3 -- 1.42 X 10 -l yr -l) from two gabbroic sills in the Tsezotene Forma- tion which are probably related to intrusions that cut the 'ba- sinal sequence' and at least as high as the overlying 'grain- stone subunit' (R. L. Armstrong et al., manuscript in preparation 1980; J. D. Aitken, personal communication, 1979). Young et al. [1979] assign the Little Dal Group to a su- pra-regional sequence deposited between  1.2 and 0.8 Ga ago. All the major units of the Helikian succession save H 1 were sampled, as well as possible correlatives in the Brock Inlier (Figure 2); but only results from the Little Dal Group are pre- sented here. Major folding occurred in the Helikian succes- sion of the Mackenzie Mountains in Paleocene or pre-late Cretaceous times. Displacements of the Little Dal Group at the Mackenzie Mountain Front relative to the Canadian Shield are estimated to have been less than 10 km in total [Ait- ken et al., 1980]. An uncon- formity above the Little Dal Group [Eisbacher, 1978] supposedly marks the beginning of the Hadrynian succession, which in part includes the remaining rock units of the Mac- kenzie Mountains Supergroup-the Redstone River and Cop- percap Formations. The Rapitan Group, separated from the Coppercap Formation by a profound unconformity [Ga- brielse, 1967], is thought to be equivalent to the Windermere Supergroup of southwestern British Columbia. Sedimentation of the Belt-Purcell and Windermere rocks probably took place within the broad limits of about 1600 to 850 Ma and 850 to 570 Ma respectively [Gabrielse, 1972; Hofmann and Aitken, 1979]. Together with previously published palcomagnetic data from Africa, the new data showed that no great relative movements have occurred between the Congo and Kalahari cratons during the interval of Pan-African tectonism in the Damara belt (McE!- hinny and McWilliams, 1977). Together with previously published palcomagnetic data from Africa, the new data showed that no great relative movements have occurred between the Congo and Kalahari cratons during the interval of Pan-African tectonism in the Damara belt (McE!- hinny and McWilliams, 1977). Continental collision preceded by large relative displacements and closure of a wide ocean (e.g., a Himalayan analog) is effectively ruled out for the Damara belt. We develop an alternative model consistent with the available palcomagnetic and geologic data, which invokes rifting, heating, and stretching of the lithosphere underneath the Damara belt, followed by delamination of the subcrustal lithosphere. Hot asthenospheric material rises to take the place of the detached and sinking lithospheric base, inducing subduction and interstacking of continental crust. Cox 1 Paleomagnetic field directions from the basalt of Pack Sack Lookout are compared to those from the Pomona Member of the Saddle Mountains Basalt of the Columbia River Basalt Group. The Pomona crops out over a wide region on the Columbia Plateau east of the Cascade Range, and the basalt of Pack Sack Lookout crops out well to the west of the Cascades about 30 to 60 km east of the Washington coast. Our paleomagnetic results support existing geologic and geochemical evidence that both these units are part of a single 12-m.y.-old flow that erupted in western Idaho and flowed to the Washington coast. The magnetic data further indicate that s9uthwest Washington has undergone clockwise rotation with respect to the Columbia Plateau and stable North America. The data suggest that both a large-scale regional rotation of--16 ø and locally complex small-scale rotations exist, the two being present to different degrees in the eastern and western regions of southwest Washington. The older magnetization, which predates Late Jurassic deformation of the volcanic arc terrane comprising the Seven Devils Group, was probably acquired in Late Triassic time. The inclinations of both normal and reversed polarity magnetizations indicate that the Triassic rocks originated approximately 18 ø from the palcoequator. The results are consistent with palcomagnetic data from similar Triassic rock assemblages on Vancouver Island and in south central Alaska. We interpret these assemblages as displaced fragments of Wrangellia, a once coherent late Paleozoic volcanic arc and early Mesozoic volcanic plateau that was torn apart and carried north by plate motion along the continental margin. We interpret the younger magnetization, which fails the fold test, as a widespread thermochemical overprint caused by Late Jurassic and Early Cretaceous plutonism. This magnetization yields a palcomagnetic pole at 60øN, 295øE (a95 = 7ø), and is similar to the pole obtained from plutons that intrude the Seven Devils Group. The angular difference between the pole from the plutons and the Late Jurassic-Early Cretaceous reference pole for stable North America suggests that the Seven Devils volcanic arc has undergone a large clockwise rotation (66 ø _+ 21ø). GEOLOGIC SUMMARY The structural setting of the southernmost Sierra Nevada is complex. The region is near the junctions of several structural-tectonic provinces: Sierra Nevada-Great Valley block, Mojave block, Basin and Range province, Salinian block, and Transverse Ranges (Figure 1). Unlike the north- em and central parts of the Sierran batholith, which are nearly devoid of major faults, the southern part is cut by numerous faults and, at least in late Cenozoic time, has probably experienced some internal deformation rather than behaving as a rigid block. This region of the Sierra Nevada is bounded on the south by the Garlock fault and on the west by the San Andreas fault and is cut by the Pleito thrust and the Kern Canyon, Edison, White Wolf, Breckenridge, and Sierra Nevada faults. The basement of the southernmost Sierra Nevada com- prises metamorphic terranes of both continental and oceanic affinities intruded by upper Cretaceous tonalite, granodio- rite, and granite plutons and minor mafic intrusives of the Sierra Nevada magmatic arc [Ross, 1980]. Three partly synchronous lava sections east of the drill site are predominantly normally magnetized and are stratigraphically of the same age as lavas dated (K-Ar) at about 9 to 10.5 m.y. (McDougall et al., 1976). The age range and magnetic properties of these lavas, the landward equivalents to marine magnetic anomaly 5 (epoch 9), suggest that several reversely magnetized lavas in one of the investigated sections were remagnetized by a 10 m thick dyke. The data presented suggest that in fresh lavas with low Curie temperatures, relatively thick dykes (about 10 m) may cause thermal overprinting of the host rocks to a distance from the dyke equal to its thickness. These results are in contrast with the generally accepted thesis that dykes affect host rocks only up to about 1 /5 of their thickness. No systematic decrease in magnetic intensity with depth was observed for a 0.9 km thick vertical lava section in Holmatindur, about 13.5 km east of the drill site. It is suggested that the heterogeneity of the lava pile in terms of magnetic intensity reflects primarily the distinct geochemistry and/or grain size of magnetic phases of individual lavas. IN

Watkins and Walker [ 1977] report how normal remanent mag- netization for the exposed basalt lava succession in eastern Iceland decreases linearly with depth below the preerosional plateau sur- face as a result of increased paleotemperature conditions. They derived this relationship from (1) the work on opaque mineralogy in eastern Iceland by A de-Hall et al. [1972] and (2)work by Walker [1960] on zeolite grade alteration. They found that for rocks demagnetized under peak alternating field conditions of 100 to 125 Oe, the magnetic intensity decreased nonlinearly with depth and approached a constant value at sea level approximately 1500 m below the preerosional plateau surface. In summary, the present study does indicate that magnetic intensity of lavas in eastern Iceland decreases neither to the extent nor in the manner reported by Watkins and Walker [1977]. If, indeed, magnetic intensity decreases with depth, the heterogeneity of the lava succ

vals in upper H olmatindur are caused by remagnetization and (2) if prior to remagnetization these lavas had normal magnetic polarities, it follows that this lava sequence would correlate perfectly with the magnetostratigraphy of the surrounding area, i.e., normal lava flows of anomaly 5 age. Second, it follows that the reversely magnetized dyke (RF-5 I D) most likely intruded the upper section after the duration of mag- netic anomaly 5, about 9 m.y. ago, i.e., long after the Holmatindur lava pile was formed. An explanation offered for the remagnetiza- tion assumes that prior to alteration of the lava pile some of the lavas had low Curie points (perhaps 300ø C). Upon intrusion of the dyke, during a reversed polarity interval, the magma temperature was high enough to cause the host lavas to reheat above their Curie points and partly or completely remagnetize some of the host lavas to distances of at least 10 m from the dyke. INTRODUCTION Devonian paleomagnetic results obtained from northern Appalachians have been interpreted in terms of a regional transcurrent motion during mid-Paleozoic time [Morris, 1976; Kent and Opdyke, 1978, 1979, 1980; Van der Voo et al., 1979]. Other alternatives such as rapid apparent polar wander during Siluro-Devonian time [Lapointe, 1979; Roy et al., 1979], and possible presence of a southerly shear zone adjoining the southeastern margin of Iapetus [Rao et al., 1981] are also explored. Roy and Anderson [1981] have discussed different alternatives to interpret the data and the difficulties in establishing both the rock and remanence ages. After this paper was submitted for publication, Roy [1982] proposed the possibility of a systematic age progression (from Ordovician to Devonian) of paleolatitudes for northern Appalachians based on the simplest possible polar path approach while Kent and Opdyke [ 1982] have disagreed with such a displacement history. MAGNETIC MINERALOGY Magnetic mineralogy of the three rock types was identified by polished section examination of twelve representative samples with a Reichert reflecting microscope (magnifica- tion 150 to 700). The metasediments contain a small quantity of fine-grained magnetite highly dispersed in the ground mass; very little hematite has been seen. In the hornfels, very fine rounded grains of magnetite are present. At sites around the edge of the contact aureole, pyrite and pyrrhotite are the additional opaque minerals commonly observed both in metasediments and hornfels. In granites, magnetite is present in large rounded grains clustering around rutile and occasionally with ilmenite. The time of remanence acquisition is the crucial issue in this debate. To examine fur- ther this issue and the general problem of the origin of hematite in red beds, we have under- taken a combined paleomagnetic, rock magnetic, and petrographic study of a red bed deposit, the Keweenawan Copper Harbor Conglomerate. Because many red beds contain more than one stable component of magnetization [Roy and Park, 1972; Turner and Ixer, 1977; Van der Voo et al., 1978; Henry, 1979; and numerous others] and more than one type of hematite [e.g., Walker et al., 1981], an important objective in the study of such beds is isolation of the different compon- ents and identification of their magnetic carriers. In particular, distinguishing a detrital remanent magnetization (DRM) from any secondary or chemical remanent magnetizations (CRM's) has obvious implications in a paleo- magnetic study. Studies of DRM have demon- strated that it can be complex, affected by a number of depositional and postdepositional processe

equate. The existence of a bedding error in cross- stratified sandstones, however, demonstrates that such beds should not be used for deposi- tional pole calculations. There are problems even with horizontally laminated sandstones, since 'inclination' erros [King, 1955] are possible. Because of these problems with sand- stones, some workers suggest that poles should be calculated from siltstone and claystone [Elston and Purucker, 1979]. Yet the magnetiza- tions in these lithologies can undergo postdepo- sitional changes and can also be of secondary origin. If such lithologies are to be used, then conglomerate and synsedimentary fold tests should be performed to determine if the remanence is contemporaneous with deposition [e.g., Purucker et al., 1980]. Although a DRM in sandstones may be of questionable value for depositional paleo- pole calculations, it accurately records polar- ity and can be used in magnetostratigraphic studies [Elston and Purucker, 1979]. Although our paleomagnetic evidence points to only one component residing in hematite, petro- graphic observations demonstrated the presence of abundant grains that are of probable detrital origin (predominantly martite) as well as authi- genic hematite. The Carboniferous geology of the eastern margin of North America suggests continent-continent collision [Hatcher, 1978]. Evidence of plutonism associated with the subducted continental crust is apparent in the large number of Carboniferous age intrusive bodies that have been located in the eastern Piedmont region (Figure 1). The postmetamorphic plutons that define two parallel linear trends (a major eastern and smaller western group) along the southeastern margin of North America have been examined in detail structurally and petrographically [Speer et al., 1980]. These plutons appear to be a supergroup similar in age and petrographic character; a common origin of these plutons is suspected. The linearity of the belts of granite plutons suggests generation of magma above a subduction zone [Fullagar and 2327 2328 BARTON AND BROWN: PALEOMAGNETISM, NORTH CAROLINA Fig 1. The plutons in this part of the Piedmont were emplaced after the late Paleozoic metamorphism and penetrative regional deformation but before the intrusion of diabase dikes, the uplift, and the erosion that occured during the Mesozoic [Butler, 1966; Butler and Ragland, 1969; Jones and Walker, 1973; Bell et al., 1974; Speer et al., 1980]. The Lilesville pluton has been dated by Fullagar and Butler [1979] at 325.27 m.y. Examination of the petrographic relationship between the gabbro and granite facies of the pluton shows that the granite had not completely cooled at the time of the gabbro intrusion [Speer et al., 1980]. Fragments of fine-grained 'pillowlike' inclusions of gabbro in the granite point to a con- temporaneous intrusion of the two magmas. Although no specific age date is available for the Pee Dee gabbro, its magmatic relationship to the Lilesville granite supports a similar early Carbonferous age. Churchland pluton. The Churchland granite is a late Pa!eozoic pluton located in the northern part of the Charlotte Belt of the Appalachian Piedmont (Figure 3). The Charl

- sedimentary and meta-igneous rocks of the Charlotte Belt are intruded by both premetamorphic and postmetamorphic plutons. The Churchland is one of the postmetamorphic plutons and believed to be part of the same magma series that produced the Lilesville, Pageland, Clouds Creek, and several other postmetamorphic granitic plutons in the southern Ap- palachians [Fullagar and Butler, 1979]. The Churchland belongs to a western group of plutons that is distinguished from an eastern group on the basis of western location and a higher Sr content. Again, the Churchland pluton is clearly younger than the regional metamorphism of the area. Petrographic studies by Privett [1973] on the Churchland con- firm that it is undeformed. Based on K/Ar analysis of whole rock and biotite samples, the age of the Churchland is 282 _+ 6 m.y. [Fullagar and Butler, 1979]. PALEoMAGNETIC STUDIES A portable gasoline-powered rock drill was used for the col- lection of paleomagnetic samples. The 2.5-cm-diameter cores were drilled in well-exposed outcrops where there was little sign of weathering. Spacing between cores was usually 50 cm, and cores were drilled to a depth of 5-10 cm. All cores were cut to 2.5-cm lengths with a rock saw. Usual- ly, only one specimen was obtained per core. The natural

The natural remanent magnetization (NRM) of each sample was measured on a Princeton Applied Research (PAR) spinner magnetometer. In order to isolate the characteristic magnetic directions, alternating field (af) demagnetization experiments were performed on representative samples from each site of the bodies sampled using a Schonstedt demagnetizer. Specimens were subject to progressively higher alternating fields in seven steps from 2.5 to 100 mT and remeasured after each treatment. MAGNETIC MINERALOGY Pee Dee/Lilesville complex. Reflection microscopy of selected samples of the Pee Dee gabbro and Lilesville granite was done to determine the oxide minerals carrying the characteristic magnetism of this body. The plutons in this part of the Piedmont were emplaced after the late Paleozoic metamorphism and penetrative regional deformation but before the intrusion of diabase dikes, the uplift, and the erosion that occured during the Mesozoic [Butler, 1966; Butler and Ragland, 1969; Jones and Walker, 1973; Bell et al., 1974; Speer et al., 1980]. Examination of the petrographic relationship between the gabbro and granite facies of the pluton shows that the granite had not completely cooled at the time of the gabbro intrusion [Speer et al., 1980]. Fragments of fine-grained 'pillowlike' inclusions of gabbro in the granite point to a con- temporaneous intrusion of the two magmas. The Churchland granite is a late Pa!eozoic pluton located in the northern part of the Charlotte Belt of the Appalachian Piedmont (Figure 3). The Charl

- sedimentary and meta-igneous rocks of the Charlotte Belt are intruded by both premetamorphic and postmetamorphic plutons. The Churchland is one of the postmetamorphic plutons and believed to be part of the same magma series that produced the Lilesville, Pageland, Clouds Creek, and several other postmetamorphic granitic plutons in the southern Ap- palachians [Fullagar and Butler, 1979]. The Churchland belongs to a western group of plutons that is distinguished from an eastern group on the basis of western location and a higher Sr content. Again, the Churchland pluton is clearly younger than the regional metamorphism of the area. Petrographic studies by Privett [1973] on the Churchland con- firm that it is undeformed. Based on K/Ar analysis of whole rock and biotite samples, the age of the Churchland is 282 _+ 6 m.y. [Fullagar and Butler, 1979]. Petrologic studies of mafic plutonic rocks in the southern Appalachians imply that the Carolina Slate Belt originated as an island arc [Butler and Fullagar, 1978; Whitney et al., 1978]. The low initial 87 Sr786 Sr ratios detected in several late Paleozoic grantic plutons of the eastern Piedmont, thought to be the result of contamination by partial melting of mafic lower crust, support the island arc model. This interpretation does not permit a Grenville age for the basement rock of the eastern Piedmont. The stratigraphic interval containing the polarity transition in the remanent magnetic field is about 1.0 m. All specimens were thermally demagnetized at 500 ø, 550 ø, 620 ø, and 660øC and show directions of magnetization of normal, reversed, and transitional character as well as a remarkable decrease of the remanent intensity in the transition zone. Wisniowiecki, Rob Van der Voo, Chad McCabe, and William C. Kelly Department of Geological Sciences, The University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan 48109 Abstract. One hundred eighty-eight oriented samples of the Late Cambrian Bonneterre carbonates of southeastern Missouri were taken from Viburnum Trend mines and local surface outcrops. Initial natural remanent magnetization directions have south- southeasterly declinations and downward inclinations. Progressive demagnetizations using thermal and AF techniques give two directions: one is a viscous present-day field direction, and the other is of reversed polarity, with south-southeasterly declinations and very shallow inclinations. The resulting paleopole, at 43øN, 126øE, is located near the Pennsylvanian to Early Permian segment of the North American apparent polar wander path. A negative conglomerate test supports this assignment for the magnetization age. Magnetic extracts from the mineralized as well as unmineralized zones of the Bonneterre contain spherical crystal aggregates of pure magnetite of late diagenetic origin. The secondary magnetization

rly Permian segment of the North American apparent polar wander path. A negative conglomerate test supports this assignment for the magnetization age. Magnetic extracts from the mineralized as well as unmineralized zones of the Bonneterre contain spherical crystal aggregates of pure magnetite of late diagenetic origin. The secondary magnetization resides in the magnetite spheroids, and we infer that the spheroids formed prior to sulfide mineralization. Introduction Diagenetic processes occurring in intracratonic basin environments are difficult to date by either stratigraphic or geochronological methods. The Cambrian Bonneterre Formation of southeastern Missouri presents an example of a carbonate sequence that underwent multiple stages of diagenesis, including mineralization of epithermal Mississippi Valley Type (MVT) deposits. Study of these deposits since the early 1800's has not solved the fundamental problem of the age of the MVT deposits, and the origin of the mineralizing fluids remains obscure. Relative age relationships of ore and gangue mineral deposition can be derived through careful study on a local scale, but determining limits on the absolute age of regional mineralization has thus far proved futile. Relative age relationships of ore and gangue mineral deposition can be derived through careful study on a local scale, but determining limits on the absolute age of regional mineralization has thus far proved futile. SAMPLING AND MEASURING TECHNIQUES In the subtropical environment of Central America, it is difficult to find suitable outcrops. Most of our sampling sites are located at places where the action of water or man provided a reasonably fresh outcrop (Figure 1). In southern Nicaragua we collected 82 samples at four sites, and in Costa Rica we drilled 324 samples at 14 sites. All but one site lie in the Pacific coastal zone because only this area has been mapped to any detail, it is accessible, and the oldest rocks seem to be restricted to this zone, at least on the sur- face. The 130-site virtual geomagnetic poles show no significant elongation and suggest no significant apparent polar wander (APW) during the period of magnetization of the igneous cen- ters. Postmagnetization structural complications in these rocks are minimal. The presence of a single predominant polarity in these intrusive complexes reinforces the radiometric age data that suggest that igneous activity within indi- vidual centers was of short duration. The north- central Montana data together with other early Tertiary, Cretaceous, and mid-Tertiary paleomag- netic results require modification of our earlier APW chronology [Diehl et al., 1980]. It now ap- pears that APW relative to North America since the Early Cretaceous consists of a polar still- stand during much of the Cretaceous (120-75 m.y. Although McElhinny [1973] lists seven early Tertiary pole positions, APW during this time interval is imprecisely known because very few of these poles were based on enough sampling sites to be considered relia- ble. As pointed out by Butler and Taylor [1978], this interval of large apparent pole migration is also coincident with the Laramide orogeny, and therefore detailed knowledge of the behavior of the apparent pole during the early Tertiary is essential in order to determine the degree to which this orogenic event is reflected in the APW path. Irving and Park [1972] have already shown that \"hairpins\" in the North American apparent polar wander path correlate with orogenic events resulting from plate interactions. It has been one of the more perplexing problems in recent palcomagnetic research that different groups, working on samples that are often from identical sections, find evidence that supports, on the one hand, rapid acqusition of stable remanence and, on the other hand, long-term acquisition. A detailed study of 203 cores constituting a grid of samples taken from a normal to reverse transition zone at the Red Grade section shows that the transition is characterized by a fairly smooth 180 ø direction change accompanied by an intensity decrease in about 80 cm of section. The transition occurs in the same way in all vertical columns within the grid and in other columns at the same stratigraphic level up to 80 m from the grid and appears identical to the transition reported by Herrero-Bervera and Helsley at the same lithologic horizon about 1 km from the grid. The intensity of NRM was quite low, usually between 8 x 10 -7 and 3 x 10 -6 emu/cm 3. The weakness of magnetization dictated caution in the magnetic cleaning of the samples. Each specimen was progressively de- magnetized by 25- or 50-Oe steps in an alternating magnetic field (af) to at least 400-Oe peak field strength. The af demag- netization removed overprinting components of secondary magnetization from most specimens and isolated their primary magnetization. Trial thermal demagnetizations were per- formed on second specimens from cores for which af cleaning data already existed. INTRODUCTION Upper Mesozoic and lower Cenozoic rocks in California can be conveniently lumped into three petrogenetic groups: (1) intrusive and extrusive crystalline and associated high- temperature metamorphic rocks of sialic arc sequences, for example, the Sierra Nevada batholith, (2) arkosic sediments of forearc sequences, for example, the Great Valley sequence, and (3) a heterogeneous assemblage of graywacke, limestone, chert, greenstone, and high-pressure metamorphic rocks of subduc- tion complexes, for example, the Franciscan assemblage. This triad represents a type example for the arc-trench-gap model of Dickinson [1970]. In map pattern, rocks of these three cate- gories fall generally into three parallel, northwest trending belts. The one obvious departure from this geometric pattern is the apparent doubling up of two such triad sequences in cen- tral California. These strata are at least 1000 m thick and represent inner to middle fan environ- ments of a submarine fan complex [Howell et al., 1977; Morgan, 1981]. The age of the sedimentary rocks at Point San Pedro has been an object of some confusion. They originally were regarded as a basal member of the Franciscan Forma- tion by Lawson [1895], but later Darrow [1963] found the strata contained early Tertiary mollusks and divided it into a Late Cretaceous lower part and Paleocene upper part. Most recent age assignments, from clams and gastropods in particu- lar, are Paleocene (Ynezian) for the entire sequence [Morgan, 1981]. The rocks at Point San Pedro are extensively faulted and folded. The strata are divisible into three fault-bounded blocks of uncertain lateral correlation [Morgan, 1981-1. In the Shelter Cove area, where we sampled, the exposure is good, and the structure is complex and consists of alternating sequences of upright and overturned thin-bedded turbidites, folded around subhorizontal axes. Upper Jurassic and Lower Cretaceous strata in the Darby and Absaroka thrust sheets were sampled in order to paleomagnetically evaluate thrust sheet rotation in the Wyoming-Idaho overthrust belt. No significant rotations were found. Lack of rotation in these thrust sheets suggests that previously reported rotation of the Prospect thrust sheet was not transmit- ted to the older Darby and Absaroka thrust sheets, indicating that the Prospect thrust sheet only exper- ienced local rotations in response to collision with the Teton-Gros Ventre uplift. Introduction Paleomagnetism was recognized early on as a tech- nique that could document thrust sheet rotation in mobile belts [e.g., Kotasek and Krs, 1965]. Sites were chosen to yield a north-south distribution in order to adequately sample the change in structural trend of the Wyoming Salient. Upper Jurassic sites (1-7) are in the Oxfordian Stump Formation [Imlay, 1952], which consists of glauconitic sandstones and siltstones, calcareous sandstones and oolitic limestones; they are the youngest Jurassic mar- ine beds in this area (Figure 2). The Ephraim Conglomerate is the lowest formation in the Gannett Group (Figure 2), a sequence that overlies the Stump Formation and that is believed to span the Jurassic-Cretaceous boundary [Eyer, 1969]. Introduction Paleomagnetism was recognized early on as a tech- nique that could document thrust sheet rotation in mobile belts [e.g., Kotasek and Krs, 1965]. After com- pleting a seminar in palcomagnetism and the University of Michigan geology field course at Camp Davis, Wyoming, then-graduate student S. Tom Crough was the first to collect palcomagnetic samples in the Wyoming- Idaho overthrust belt near Camp Davis. Tom worked on this pilot collection for one semester, and his results were later incorporated in a publication [Grubbs and Van der Voo, 1976]. A decade later, we have returned to the area for a follow-up paleomagnetic study of thrust sheet rotations. We wish to dedicate this paper to the memory of Tom. Traces of the major thrust sheets in the northern overthrust belt of western Wyoming and eastern Idaho strike N-S through most of Wyoming and Idaho, chang- ing strike to a NW-SE orientation just south of Jackson, Wyoming (Figure 1). The origin of this curvature has been the s

48-0227/84/004B-059 5505.00 Wyoming salient [Grubbs and Van der Voo, 1976] indi- cated that systematic rotation of thrust sheets develop- ed in response to their impingement upon the buttress- es. Portions of the thrust sheets in the vicinity of the basement uplifts rotated counterclockwise in the north- ern region, where they encountered the ancestral Teton-Gros Ventre block, and clockwise in the southern region, where their motion was impeded by the Game Hill high-angle reverse fault (Figure 1). The rotated sites of Grubbs and Van der Voo [1976] are almost exclusively in the frontal Prospect thrust sheet (Figure 1), while those sites located on the Darby and Absaroka thrust sheets to the west show little or no rotation. In this study, Upper Jurassic and Lower Cret- aceous strata on these westward thrust sheets were sampled to determine whether they have rotated also. Sampling and Geology Seven to eleven oriented samples were taken per site from five formations using a portable hand-held rock drill. These samples were then cut into one or more specimens for analysis. Ten sites (5-14) were located in the Absaroka thrust sheet, three (2-4) in the Darby thrust sheet, and one (1) in the Bear thrust sheet, a splay off the frontal Prospect thrust sheet (Figure 1).
